nameStory: Clinton's Bulrush is named after George William Clinton, a 19th-century American botanist who explored the flora of New York State. Despite its common name suggesting it's a bulrush, this plant actually belongs to a different group called deergrasses, showing how common names can sometimes be misleading in the plant world.
description: Clinton's Bulrush is a small, clumping sedge that grows up to 16 inches tall in wetlands and boggy areas. This perennial forms dense tufts without spreading underground stems, creating neat little colonies. It has narrow, grass-like leaves and produces small brown flower clusters at the tips of triangular stems. Though called a bulrush, it's actually more closely related to cotton grass and other deergrasses.

idTips.label: Stems
idTips.description: Feel the stem between your fingers - it's distinctly triangular in cross-section rather than round, with three sharp edges you can easily detect by rolling it gently

idTips.label: Flowers
idTips.description: Look for a single small brown spikelet at the tip of each stem, containing just 3-6 tiny flowers - much smaller and simpler than typical bulrush flower clusters

idTips.label: Growth Habit
idTips.description: Forms dense, compact clumps without spreading runners, creating isolated tufts rather than expansive colonies like many other wetland sedges

idTips.label: Leaves
idTips.description: Narrow, grass-like leaves up to 10 inches long that feel smooth and slightly stiff to the touch, growing from the base of the plant

idTips.label: Seeds
idTips.description: Produces tiny flattened triangular seeds about the size of a pinhead, brown and hard when mature

habitat: Look for Clinton's Bulrush in acidic wetlands, particularly sphagnum bogs, wet meadows, and marshy areas throughout northern New England. It prefers nutrient-poor, peaty soils and is often found growing alongside bog plants like cranberries, pitcher plants, and other specialized wetland sedges.

seasonality.spring: New green shoots emerge from the base, and triangular stems begin to elongate as the growing season starts.
seasonality.summer: Flowering occurs with small brown spikelets appearing at stem tips, followed by seed development in late summer.
seasonality.fall: Seeds ripen and disperse while leaves begin to yellow and die back, though some foliage may persist.
seasonality.winter: Above-ground parts die back completely, leaving only the root system alive underground until spring regrowth.

funFact: With only 4 recorded observations in all of New England, Clinton's Bulrush is one of the region's rarest sedges - you're more likely to spot a moose than find this elusive little plant!
confusionNotes: Most likely confused with other small sedges in wetlands, but the combination of triangular stems, single brown spikelet per stem, and clumping growth habit without runners distinguishes it from common sedges like three-way sedge which has multiple flower clusters.
contextualKnowledge: The name 'bulrush' is confusing here because true bulrushes belong to a different genus (Scirpus) and look quite different. Clinton's Bulrush is actually in the deergrass genus, reflecting how common names don't always match botanical relationships.
compareHints: Clinton's Bulrush differs from its relative Tufted Bulrush by forming denser clumps and lacking the cottony bristles that other deergrasses often have. Unlike Cotton Deergrass, it doesn't produce the fluffy white seed heads, and compared to Bashful Bulrush, it has more upright growth rather than creeping stems.

relatedSpecies.distinction: Tufted bulrush differs from its Trichophorum relatives by its distinctive cushion-forming growth habit – cotton deergrass grows in loose colonies rather than tight tufts, while bashful bulrush has broader leaves and a more upright stance.
Among its Trichophorum relatives, Cotton Deergrass is distinguished by its extremely short leaves and prominent white bristles.

Bashful Bulrush is much smaller and more delicate than its Trichophorum relatives - while Tufted Bulrush forms dense, robust clumps and Cotton Deergrass has distinctive white, fluffy seed heads, Bashful Bulrush stays low and inconspicuous.
